The encoding is used to produce safe JS string literals for inline onclick attributes — this pattern is correct and the flag converts silent failures to thrown exceptions. No blocking issues.

comments.note: The JSON encoding pattern is architecturally correct: json_encode() is used to produce JS string literals for inline onclick attributes. JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR converts the silent false return (on encoding failure) into a \JsonException. For plain PHP strings (which $urlTemplate and $inputId always are), encoding never fails — so this adds a safety net with zero runtime cost.

The \JsonException is not caught at the call site and will propagate up. This is intentional and correct for a library — producing broken HTML with the literal 'false' injected into a JS onclick attribute would be a silent failure far worse than a thrown exception. No change needed.

The two encoding targets ($urlTemplate from getPageURLTemplate() and $inputId a concatenated grid/element ID string) are both plain PHP strings. JSON encoding them produces valid JS string literals with all necessary escaping handled by PHP's json_encode(). This is the secure approach for injecting PHP values into inline JS — correct and consistent across both renderers.
